## What the model says

In a ranking task the observer puts `m` items in order by their evidence, and the datum is the rank the target
receives ([Meyer-Grant et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000615)). The target draws its evidence from a
distribution located at `d`, each of the `m` − 1 lures from the same distribution located at 0. The target gets
rank `r` when exactly `r` − 1 lures have more evidence than it, so rank 1 is the target ahead of every lure. There is
no criterion. With $f_T$ the target's density and $F$ the lures' cumulative distribution function (the chance that
one lure falls below $x$), the probability that `r` − 1 lures lie above the target's evidence $x$ and `m` − `r` below
it, added up over every $x$, is

$$
P(\text{rank } r) = \binom{m - 1}{r - 1} \int f_T(x)\, F(x)^{m - r}\, \bigl(1 - F(x)\bigr)^{r - 1}\, dx ,
$$

where the binomial coefficient counts which of the lures are the ones above. Rank 1
is the m-alternative forced-choice event, so with equal SDs P(rank 1) equals P(correct) of the
[m-AFC model](sdt_mafc.qmd) with the same `d` and `dist`. `sdt_ranking()` offers two distributions. Under `gumbel_min`, bmm's default, the integral
has a closed form. Under `normal`, bmm sums it over fixed points (numerical quadrature), and this page uses the
same points, so its numbers are bmm's; `normal` adds `sdratio`, the target's SD over the lures'. Then `d` is
$d_a$, the distance between the two locations over the root mean square of the two SDs, which keeps P(rank 1) at
`m` = 2 equal to $\Phi(d/\sqrt{2})$, $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function, for every `sdratio`. A row of data holds how often the target got each rank,
which is multinomial with these probabilities.

## The task

One trial shows `m` items, one of them the target, for instance a studied word among `m` − 1 new ones, and the
participant puts all `m` in order, from the most to the least likely target. bmm fits counts: each row of the data
holds, in one column per rank, the number of trials in which the target received that rank. The number of items
`m` is the task setting that enters the likelihood: it sets how many ranks there are and how many lures can push
the target down. `sdt_ranking()` takes it as a number, or as the name of a data column when it varies between rows;
a row with fewer items than count columns leaves the surplus columns at 0.

## Explore

In the task panel, the tiles show the `m` items of one trial (the orange one is the target, which the observer
does not know) and below them one possible order, with the target placed second. Next to them are the evidence
densities of the target (orange) and of one lure (dashed grey). The panel "Predicted" gives the probability of
each rank for the target at the current values: with `d` above 0 the first ranks gain, and the last rank is the
target falling behind every lure. Under `normal`, `sdratio` above 1 widens the target's distribution, so it lands
more often at either end of the order.

The `d` slider spans bmm's default prior for `d`, normal(1, 1) (mean 1, SD 1), from mean − 3 SD to mean + 3 SD (−2
to 4), and starts at the prior mean, 1 (dashed outlines). The `sdratio` slider spans bmm's prior for its log,
normal(0, 0.3), over the same ± 3 SD (a ratio from 0.41 to 2.46), on a log scale; the box shows the ratio. bmm
holds it at 1 unless the formula names it. `m` runs from 2 to 8.

## Across task settings

`m` is the design variable of this model. With `d` fixed, the target is less often first as `m` grows, because more
lures can beat it, and the probability spreads over more ranks. The panel "Across m" draws P(rank 1) and P(rank
`m`), the last rank, at every `m`, with the ranks in between as grey dots and chance, 1/`m`, dotted. The other
distribution is drawn dashed at its own `d`: the one that gives it the same P(rank 1) as the solid line at the
current `m` (the circle), found by the page and named in the legend. P(rank 1)
is all that an m-AFC task records, and at one `m` either distribution can match it. The other ranks are where they
part: at the start, both at `d` = 1, `gumbel_min` and `normal` give the same first rank to two decimals (0.550
and 0.552), but the last rank 0.109 and 0.068. This is why ranking data say more about the shape of the
evidence distribution than forced-choice accuracy does
([Meyer-Grant et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000615)), even at a single `m`.

The code updates with the controls. `sdt_ranking()` names the count columns, the number of items and the evidence
distribution, `dsdt_ranking()` returns the log likelihood of a row of rank counts, and `bmm()` estimates `d` (and,
under `normal`, `sdratio` when the formula names it) from data; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs
Stan through brms. See the [signal detection article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_sdt.html) and the
reference pages for [`sdt_ranking()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_ranking.html) and
[`dsdt_ranking()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_ranking_dist.html).
